question:
A previously healthy 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of a recurring rash that typically occurs on exposure to the sun and affects only the face. She also has noticed several nonpainful ulcers on the roof of her mouth. She is sexually active with one male partner and they use condoms inconsistently. Her mother has end-stage renal disease. The patient does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows an erythematous rash across the cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds. There are three small ulcers on the hard palate. Laboratory studies show:
Leukocyte count 3,000/mm3
Platelet count 70,000/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 80 mm/h
Serum
Antinuclear antibodies 1:320
Anti-Smith antibodies positive
Urine
Protein 3+
RBC casts negative
RBCs none
WBCs 10–15/hpf
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Positive antinuclear antibodies and anti-Smith antibodies -> suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) -> 80% CHAIN: Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia -> common findings in SLE -> 70% CHAIN: Proteinuria and hematuria -> indicate possible renal involvement in SLE -> 75% CHAIN: Erythematous rash across the cheeks sparing nasolabial folds -> classic malar rash in SLE -> 85% CHAIN: Small ulcers on the hard palate -> may indicate mucosal involvement in SLE -> 70% CHAIN: Given the clinical presentation and laboratory findings suggestive of SLE -> consider skin biopsy to confirm the diagnosis -> 80%
enhanced_information: The patient's presentation with positive antinuclear antibodies, anti-Smith antibodies, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, proteinuria, and mucosal ulcers is highly suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Given the clinical and laboratory findings, the most appropriate next step in management would be a skin biopsy to confirm the diagnosis of SLE.
analysis: The patient's presentation with a malar rash, oral ulcers, positive antinuclear antibodies, anti-Smith antibodies, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and proteinuria is highly suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Given the clinical and laboratory findings, the most appropriate next step in management would be a skin biopsy to confirm the diagnosis of SLE.
